title: Marching in Step
text:
Armies drill, congregations sing, and crowds chant together. Scott Wiltermuth and Chip Heath of Stanford University wondered whether moving in unison actually changes how people treat one another.

In one experiment, small groups of students walked around campus. Some were told to walk in step, others to walk normally. In another, participants wore headphones and listened to the Canadian national anthem. Some sang along together while others just read the words silently.

Afterward, the groups played economic games in which each person could keep money for themselves or contribute to a group outcome, and in which success depended on trusting others to cooperate. Groups that had walked, sung or moved in synchrony cooperated more than groups that had not. They also reported feeling more like part of a team.

The effect appeared even though the synchronous activities were brief and the people did not necessarily feel happier afterward. Acting in unison, the authors suggested, may be one of the old ways human groups have used to bind members together.
lesson: Shared rhythm builds shared purpose. Doing something together in time, even briefly, can make a group readier to cooperate.
source: Wiltermuth, S. S., and Heath, C. (2009). Synchrony and cooperation. Psychological Science, 20(1), 1-5.
caveat: Later research suggests the effect of synchrony on cooperation is real but smaller and less consistent than this first study implied.
